framework.name: Illinois Learning Standards for Social Science, Economics 9–12, with the Council for Economic Education Voluntary National Content Standards in Economics
framework.note: Codes are Illinois 9–12 economics and financial-literacy standards (SS.EC.x.9-12, SS.EC.FL.x.9-12) and CEE national content standards (CEE 1–20); alignment was made by the course author and is not a certification by either body.

standards.text: Analyze how incentives shape choices that carry different costs and benefits for different groups
Weigh marginal benefits against marginal costs to argue for or against a solution to an economic problem
Scarcity forces individuals and societies to choose among wants, giving up alternatives
Sound decisions compare additional costs and benefits, and most choices are made at the margin
Every allocation method, market or otherwise, has advantages and disadvantages
Explain how personal goals, education and career choices shape income and financial decisions
Analyze how incentives determine what is produced and how it is distributed in a market system
People respond predictably to positive and negative incentives
Markets exist where buyers and sellers interact, and prices are set by supply and demand
Prices send signals and incentives that coordinate buyers and sellers across markets
Evaluate how well government policies that change market outcomes achieve their goals
Price changes, including those caused by controls, reshape the incentives of buyers and sellers
Government provides public goods and corrects externalities and other market failures
Government intervention can also fail when costs fall on some groups and benefits go to others
Institutions such as property rights, courts and contracts make markets work
Analyze how competition and incentives shape what firms produce and how output is distributed
The degree of competition among sellers affects prices, output and product variety
Entrepreneurs take risks to organize resources and introduce new products and methods
Corporations, banks and other institutions channel resources through the economy
Income depends on the market value of the productive resources a person supplies
Use economic indicators to judge whether government policy is improving market outcomes
Economic growth, measured by rising real GDP, comes from investment in physical and human capital and technology
Unemployment and inflation impose real costs on individuals and the economy
Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money over time
Evaluate the effectiveness of fiscal policies meant to change economic outcomes
Argue for or against a policy response using marginal costs and benefits
Economic fluctuations arise from changes in overall spending and production
Fiscal policy uses government spending and taxes to influence output, employment and prices
Political pressures can lead government policy away from economically efficient choices
Money serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value
Interest rates reflect the price of borrowing and reward for saving, adjusted for inflation
The central bank uses monetary policy to influence interest rates, inflation and employment
Weigh the costs and benefits of different forms of credit and the effect of interest
Compare saving and investment options by expected return and risk
Evaluate ways to manage financial risk, including insurance
Evaluate how taxes and trade policies alter market outcomes
Analyze how trade and tax policies create winners and losers among different groups
Voluntary exchange benefits both parties, within a nation and across borders
Specialization and comparative advantage raise output and make trade worthwhile
Taxes fund government services and shift incentives for producers and consumers
